title: Joins & INNER JOIN
html:
A join combines rows from two tables by matching a condition — usually a foreign key equal to a primary key. INNER JOIN keeps only the rows that match on both sides.

Why joins exist

Normalised tables store each fact once: an employee row holds dept_id = 1, not the text Engineering, Bengaluru. A join puts the pieces back together at query time.

JoinReturns
INNER JOINOnly matching pairs
LEFT [OUTER] JOINAll left rows + matches (NULLs where none)
RIGHT [OUTER] JOINAll right rows + matches
FULL [OUTER] JOINAll rows from both sides
CROSS JOINEvery combination (Cartesian product)
Self joinA table joined to itself (hierarchies, comparisons)

INNER JOIN

10 employees, but only 9 rows: Dev (dept_id NULL) matches no department, and Marketing matches no employee — an inner join drops both. JOIN alone means INNER JOIN.

How a join is evaluated (conceptually)

1
Pair up
Take every combination of a row from the left table with a row from the right table.
2
Keep matches
Keep only pairs for which the ON condition is true.
3
Continue
Further joins, WHERE, GROUP BY… work on this combined row set.
Key point

That is only the meaning. Physically the optimizer uses a nested-loop join (with an index on the inner side), a hash join (build a hash table on the smaller side) or a merge join (both inputs sorted on the key).

Joining several tables

ON vs USING vs NATURAL

Watch out

NATURAL JOIN joins on every column with the same name. employees NATURAL JOIN departments would match on both dept_id and name (employee name = department name) and return nothing. Avoid it — spell out the condition.

Join condition vs filter

For an inner join, a condition in ON or in WHERE gives the same result. Convention: relationships in ON, row filters in WHERE. For outer joins the placement changes the result — see the next topic.

Watch out

Forgetting the join condition (old comma syntax FROM a, b with no WHERE) creates a Cartesian product — 10 employees × 4 departments = 40 rows of nonsense. Explicit JOIN … ON makes the omission obvious.

What is the difference between JOIN and INNER JOIN?

None — INNER is optional. JOIN … ON … is an inner join.

Can you join on columns that are not keys?

Yes; any boolean condition works (ON a.city = b.city, ranges, inequalities). Joins on unindexed or non-unique columns can be slow or multiply rows, so know the cardinality of both sides.
